newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Ousted Colombian minister says nation "demonized".
newsitem.headline: Ousted Colombian minister says nation "demonized".

text.p: Defence minister Guillermo Alberto Gonzalez, who resigned on Sunday amid an emerging drug corruption scandal, said on Monday he was a victim of the "demonizing" of Colombia at home and abroad.

"The demonising of Colombia and incomprehension are what got to me," Gonzalez told a news conference, when asked about the reasons behind his sudden fall from the high office he was sworn into only last month.
He did not elaborate, except to say he had no wish to exacerbate the "serious problems" in Colombia's ties with Washington or add to the country's increasingly bad image abroad.

He used the term "witch hunt" in an earlier interview, saying public life had become virtually impossible for anyone with even the most remote ties to drug lords because of Colombia's widely perceived image as a "narco-democracy."

Gonzalez, a former diplomat and lawmaker, stepped down just two days after revealing that his congressional campaign had received a $3,000 donation from reputed drug kingpin Justo Pastor Perafan in 1989.

Gonzalez and Perafan, both in their 50s, grew up in the same town in southwest Colombia and his ties with the alleged drug lord were the target of hard-hitting reports in the local media even before he was appointed in January to succeed Juan Carlos Esquerra, who was named ambassador to Washington.

President Ernesto Samper's first defence minister, Fernando Botero, has been held at a Bogota military base since August 1995 on drug-corruption charges stemming from his involvement in the president's scandal-plagued 1994 campaign.

Gonzalez's surprising revelation about the 1989 campaign payoff -- from a man now billed as Colombia's most wanted criminal -- was widely seen as something that would further tarnish the drug-tainted image of Samper himself.

Gonzalez has repeatedly admitted having social dealings with Perafan in the past. But he also insisted that there was no reason to suspect him of criminal wrongdoing until February of last year, when a warrant was issued for his arrest on the drug-related charge of "illicit enrichment."

Perafan's net worth is estimated by Semana, Colombia's leading news magazine, at $12 billion and he is said to have business interests in Madrid, Rome and Moscow as well as throughout Colombia. Underscoring his power, and the impunity with which he built up his allegedly criminal business empire, he was decorated by Colombia's Congress for distinguished service to the business community just three years ago.

Samper had pledged his full support for Gonzalez on Friday, soon after he revealed Perafan's campaign contribution. But a senior military source told Reuters that armed forces commander Gen. Harold Bedoya issued a virtual ultimatum to Samper, telling him he and other top military officials would step down if Gonzalez remained in office.

Gonzalez had quietly criticised the military's poor human rights record, and government officials privately concede that he angered senior army officials by publicly supporting calls for deep-rooted reform of military justice.
Even before he took office, army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett took a public swipe at Gonzalez by calling him "someone who has had close ties with a delinquent."
